1.pericope_label: Now Jehoram the son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and reigned twelve years. And he wrought evil in the sight of the Lord; but not like his father, and like his mother: for he put away the image of Baal that his father had made. Nevertheless he cleaved unto the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which made Israel to sin; he departed not therefrom.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the accession formula literally, identifies the image as a pillar, and argues from the Greek plural and its added clause that Jehoram broke the pillars in pieces, explaining the survival of the cult by Jezebel's living through the reign.
Gill reckons the accession arithmetic, showing that Ahaziah's two years were not complete but ran from part of Jehoshaphat's seventeenth into part of his eighteenth.

Clarke states the reform plainly as the abolition of Baal with the calves of Dan and Beth-el retained; Wesley reads the calves politically, as a wall of partition the kings of Israel kept up between their subjects and those of Judah.

Henry indicts the reform under three heads, that it was partial in reach, partial in object since the calves remained as the state engine of the division, and partial in thoroughness since the image was laid aside rather than broken.

debates: Whether Jehoram broke the image or merely laid it aside: Henry's heaviest charge rests on the shorter Hebrew text, while Ellicott judges the Greek addition "and brake them in pieces" original.
Whether the reform was sincere or political, Henry and Wesley both tracing the retention of the calves to reasons of state.
outliers: Henry allows that the influence in the alliance may have run both ways, Jehoshaphat perhaps doing something towards making Ahab's family better even as he made his own worse.
themes: Now Jehoram the son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and reigned twelve years.
And he wrought evil in the sight of the Lord; but not like his father, and like his mother: for he put away the image of Baal that his father had made.
Nevertheless he cleaved unto the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which made Israel to sin; he departed not therefrom.

4.pericope_label: And Mesha king of Moab was a sheepmaster, and rendered unto the king of Israel an hundred thousand lambs, and an hundred thousand rams, with the wool. But it came to pass, when Ahab was dead, that the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel. And king Jehoram went out of Samaria the same time, and numbered all Israel. And he went and sent to Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, saying, The king of Moab hath rebelled against me: wilt thou go with me against Moab to battle? And he said, I will go up: I am as thou art, my people as thy people, and my horses as thy horses. And he said, Which way shall we go up? And he answered, The way through the wilderness of Edom.

schools.summary: Ellicott parses the tribute as a hundred thousand fatted lambs and the fleeces of a hundred thousand rams and calls it a heavy burden for so small a country, citing Mesha's own monument; Delitzsch establishes that it was annual and concludes the opposite, that it could not be exorbitant for a land so rich in pasture.
Gill offers three reasons why Ahaziah never reduced Moab, his temper, his sickness, or the shortness of his reign.
Clarke collects the versions on "sheepmaster" and derives the word from marking or branding flocks; Wesley makes Mesha's wealth itself the thing that enabled and emboldened the revolt.

Henry allows no excuse for the loss of the tribute and is of two minds about the alliance, admiring Jehoshaphat's magnanimity in not reopening the old revolt while warning that there is nothing got by being yoked with unbelievers.

debates: Whether the Moabite tribute was oppressive, as Ellicott holds from the figures and from Mesha's inscription, or easily borne, as Delitzsch argues from the country's pasture.
What "sheepmaster" means: Clarke derives it from the marking of sheep, Ellicott from an Arabic word for a breed of superior wool.
Why Jehoshaphat joined a king he had been rebuked for allying with, whether from magnanimity, from the need to chastise revolt before it spread to Edom, or from an old score against Moab.
outliers: Ellicott, having accepted one Greek addition two verses earlier as original, rejects the addition here as probably a transcriber's.
themes: And Mesha king of Moab was a sheepmaster, and rendered unto the king of Israel an hundred thousand lambs, and an hundred thousand rams, with the wool.
But it came to pass, when Ahab was dead, that the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel.
And king Jehoram went out of Samaria the same time, and numbered all Israel.

And he went and sent to Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, saying, The king of Moab hath rebelled against me: wilt thou go with me against Moab to battle? And he said, I will go up: I am as thou art, my people as thy people, and my horses as thy horses.
And he said, Which way shall we go up? And he answered, The way through the wilderness of Edom.

9.pericope_label: So the king of Israel went, and the king of Judah, and the king of Edom: and they fetched a compass of seven days’ journey: and there was no water for the host, and for the cattle that followed them. And the king of Israel said, Alas! that the Lord hath called these three kings together, to deliver them into the hand of Moab! But Jehoshaphat said, Is there not here a prophet of the Lord, that we may enquire of the Lord by him? And one of the king of Israel’s servants answered and said, Here is Elisha the son of Shaphat, which poured water on the hands of Elijah. And Jehoshaphat said, The word of the Lord is with him. So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom went down to him.

schools.summary: Delitzsch and Ellicott independently place the army in the Wady el Ahsy and explain the failure of the water there; Ellicott repunctuates the verse, argues the distress began only after the Edomites joined, and holds that Elisha followed the army under a divine impulse.
Gill notes that Jehoram, the principal in drawing the others in, throws the blame on the Lord and his providence, and that Jehoshaphat's question came too late.
Clarke judges the march ill planned; Wesley makes the length of it deliberate, and reads the kings' visit to the prophet's tent as an honour calculated to engage his utmost assistance.
Henry charges Jehoram with fretting against the Lord for a calamity of his own making, and observes that good men are often remiss until necessity and affliction drive them to their duty.

debates: Why the march took seven days: Clarke blames bad planning, Ellicott suspects they lost their way, and Wesley makes the wide circuit deliberate.
Whether Jehoram's cry that the Lord had called the kings together is sound theology, as Clarke takes it, or evasion, as Gill and Henry read it.
Why three kings went down to the prophet rather than summoning him: esteem, humiliation by misfortune, or calculation.
outliers: Wesley explains the office of pouring water on a master's hands as the more necessary among the Israelites because of the frequent washings their law required.
themes: So the king of Israel went, and the king of Judah, and the king of Edom: and they fetched a compass of seven days’ journey: and there was no water for the host, and for the cattle that followed them.
And the king of Israel said, Alas! that the Lord hath called these three kings together, to deliver them into the hand of Moab!

But Jehoshaphat said, Is there not here a prophet of the Lord, that we may enquire of the Lord by him? And one of the king of Israel’s servants answered and said, Here is Elisha the son of Shaphat, which poured water on the hands of Elijah.
And Jehoshaphat said, The word of the Lord is with him. So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom went down to him.

13.pericope_label: And Elisha said unto the king of Israel, What have I to do with thee? get thee to the prophets of thy father, and to the prophets of thy mother. And the king of Israel said unto him, Nay: for the Lord hath called these three kings together, to deliver them into the hand of Moab. And Elisha said, As the Lord of hosts liveth, before whom I stand, surely, were it not that I regard the presence of Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, I would not look toward thee, nor see thee. But now bring me a minstrel. And it came to pass, when the minstrel played, that the hand of the Lord came upon him. And he said, Thus saith the Lord, Make this valley full of ditches. For thus saith the Lord, Ye shall not see wind, neither shall ye see rain; yet that valley shall be filled with water, that ye may drink, both ye, and your cattle, and your beasts. And this is but a light thing in the sight of the Lord: he will deliver the Moabites also into your hand. And ye shall smite every fenced city, and every choice city, and shall fell every good tree, and stop all wells of water, and mar every good piece of land with stones. And it came to pass in the morning, when the meat offering was offered, that, behold, there came water by the way of Edom, and the country was filled with water.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes "the prophets of thy father" to include both Baal prophets and false prophets of the Lord and reads the sarcasm as evidence the former survived; he dissolves the conflict with Deuteronomy by making the verbs continuative rather than imperative, and explains the water as a storm on the mountains of Seir whose miraculous element lies in the prediction and the timing. Delitzsch describes the music as collecting the mind from the outer world, and reads the hour of the morning sacrifice as a sign of restored favour.
Gill identifies the minstrel as a Levite accustomed to the melody of David and offers three ways of reconciling the order to fell the trees with the law.

Clarke and Ellicott both cite Cicero on the Pythagoreans calming their minds with the harp, but Clarke adds the affair at Beth-el as a further cause of Elisha's agitation, makes the ditches part of a stratagem of reflected sunlight, and insists the water was altogether miraculous; Wesley has the music excite Elisha to prayer as well as calm him, and reads the timing as a testimony against the northern worship.
Henry makes the digging of the ditches a test of faith and obedience, since those who expect God's blessings must prepare room for them.

debates: Why the ditches were dug: as a stratagem of reflected light, as a means of holding water that would otherwise run off, or as a test of faith.
How the order to fell the trees stands with Deuteronomy 20:19, whether fruit trees are excluded, the law restricted, the law dispensed with, or the verbs predictive rather than imperative.
Whether the water was supplied by wholly supernatural means, as Clarke insists, or by a natural storm whose miracle lies in its prediction and timing, as Ellicott argues.
outliers: Clarke contrasts the heathen priests, thrown into violent agitations and contortions by the demons possessing them, with the true prophets, who received the word in the utmost serenity and composure.
themes: And Elisha said unto the king of Israel, What have I to do with thee? get thee to the prophets of thy father, and to the prophets of thy mother. And the king of Israel said unto him, Nay: for the Lord hath called these three kings together, to deliver them into the hand of Moab.

21.pericope_label: And when all the Moabites heard that the kings were come up to fight against them, they gathered all that were able to put on armour, and upward, and stood in the border. And they rose up early in the morning, and the sun shone upon the water, and the Moabites saw the water on the other side as red as blood: And they said, This is blood: the kings are surely slain, and they have smitten one another: now therefore, Moab, to the spoil. And when they came to the camp of Israel, the Israelites rose up and smote the Moabites, so that they fled before them: but they went forward smiting the Moabites, even in their country. And they beat down the cities, and on every good piece of land cast every man his stone, and filled it; and they stopped all the wells of water, and felled all the good trees: only in Kir–haraseth left they the stones thereof; howbeit the slingers went about it, and smote it. And when the king of Moab saw that the battle was too sore for him, he took with him seven hundred men that drew swords, to break through even unto the king of Edom: but they could not. Then he took his eldest son that should have reigned in his stead, and offered him for a burnt offering upon the wall. And there was great indignation against Israel: and they departed from him, and returned to their own land.

schools.summary: Ellicott explains the illusion by the sunrise behind the Moabites and the red earth of the locality, limits the destruction by reading the Kir-haraseth clause as its terminus, and construes the closing wrath as the wrath of Chemosh falling on the alliance, a conception he treats as a token of the record's antiquity; Delitzsch holds the sacrifice was offered to Chemosh and not to the God of Israel.

Gill devotes his note to refuting the view that the victim was the king of Edom's son, on the ground that a deputy king could have no heir with a right to succeed and that such a sacrifice would have hardened rather than raised the siege.

Clarke takes the appearance of blood for an ordinary optical deception, reports and rejects the reading that made the offering to the sun, and leaves the closing indignation between divine displeasure and the horror of the surrounding nations; Wesley has the slingers breaking down the walls rather than shooting the defenders.
Henry traces the Moabite self-deception step by step and draws from the outcome the rule that it is well not to urge the worst of men to extremities.

debates: Whose son was sacrificed, Mesha's own or a hostage son of the king of Edom.
Whose wrath the closing clause describes: the Lord's displeasure with Israel, the revulsion of the surrounding nations, or, as Ellicott argues, the wrath of Chemosh answering the sacrifice.
What the slingers were doing, shooting the defenders on the walls or battering the walls themselves.
outliers: Ellicott asks why divine wrath should fall on the involuntary cause rather than the voluntary agents, and answers that if the wrath of the Lord is meant we cannot tell.
